THE LOEVENHEIMS.

I have been interested in the Loewenheimis for more than a year, but although I have questioned many contacts about them, I have been unable to obtain a complete picture of their activities. It is undeniable that both were at one time ardent and very active communists. The most detailed report of their communistic activities comes from [redacted] who claims that during their Berlin period they were espionage agents of the Soviet Union. The nearest confirmation I can get of this is the statement of Moeller-Dostall that at one time they were "in close touch with the Comintern".

There is a consensus of opinion among my contacts that Walter Loewenheim is the dominating personality and that Ernst was always an instrument in his brother's hands. Likewise, these contacts agree that there is not much harm in Karthauser, whom they speak of as an exceedingly able engineer. This man resided for some years in Russia, where he was employed as a specialist under one of the Five Year Plans, but the general opinion is that he remained untouched by Communism.

There is also no doubt that the Loewenheimis left the Communist Party. After thinking the matter over for some time, I tend to the view that Walter Loewenheim is one of those individuals -- not infrequently found in left politics who can never remain in one party permanently, but go the round of all parties. I know just such a case in my own locality; the man in question was first a somewhat extreme member of the Labour party; then he joined the I.L.P., which he abandoned in 1935 for the Communist Party. During the last year I have noted a cooling off in his party zeal, but whether he will move right to the orthodox Labour movement or join one of the anti-Stalinist Communist groups, I cannot say.

The motives for such changes are usually quarrelsomeness or a sense of unwarped ambition. Loewenheim has often been described to me as a restless, ambitious, unscrupulous man, so that I am inclined to regard his renunciation of Stalinist Communism as due to resentment or lack of advancement rather than a genuine conversion. Evidently he thought he could do better with a show of his own; hence his participation in the foundation of Neubeginnen, which he hoped to dominate. Finding that it was impossible to oust FRANK from the leadership, he split off and founded another group in which he imagined he could be the leader. Lately he announced his intention of applying for membership of the Trade Union Centre for German Workers in Great Britain. Hans Gottrurch, the German Trade Union leader, assured me that he has not the slightest chance of getting in, because his habit of joining organisations and then leaving them is too well known.

Gottrurch likes to take a kindly view of people whenever possible. In a recent conversation with me he wondered whether it might be possible to release Walter Loewenheim if he gave his solemn word to refrain from any political activities.
